overview: The Papal States were territories governed by the pope as a temporal ruler, alongside his religious role. Their changing extent and interrupted history differ from the continuing institution of the Holy See. The atlas separates an early entry around 800 from a later one, but neither coverage boundary is a reliable foundation or fall date.

periods.title: Early papal Rome
periods.summary: Churches, mosaics and the memory of Charlemagne’s coronation illuminate early medieval Rome. The atlas’s 800 to 900 entry is only a limited slice of this longer history.

periods.title: A changing territorial state
periods.summary: Papal rule joined religious authority to government over central Italian territories. Later hospitals, libraries and waterworks served different communities under that government.

periods.title: Interruptions and territorial ending
periods.summary: French-era upheavals interrupted papal government. Italian forces captured Rome in 1870, ending the remaining territorial state; the Holy See continued.

sections.title: Early Rome and the evidence it left

items.text: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day in 800. A famous Vatican painting depicts the ceremony, but it was made in the Renaissance and gives historical figures the faces of later rulers. It is evidence for how later popes remembered the event, not an eyewitness image from 800.

Pope Paschal I rebuilt Santa Prassede in the ninth century. Reused granite columns and richly colored mosaics survive in a church that later generations repeatedly altered. Reusing older stone connected new construction to Rome’s material past; it does not make every part of the present building ancient.

The San Zeno chapel at Santa Prassede was associated with Paschal’s mother, Theodora. Its mosaics bring a named family relationship into a monumental religious setting. This was exceptional papal patronage, not evidence that ordinary mothers received comparable chapels.

The San Zeno mosaics are dated to Paschal I’s pontificate, 817 to 824, using inscriptions and written evidence. The heritage catalogue also identifies nineteenth-century restoration in papal portraits. A beautiful surviving image may contain medieval work and much later repair: dating the building is only the first step.

sections.title: Books, family care and city water

items.text: In 1475 Sixtus IV gave the Vatican Library a formal foundation and financial support, with Bartolomeo Platina as librarian. A library needed staff, rooms and money as well as manuscripts. This was a learned institution attached to papal government, not universal public education.

The Vatican Library kept rules for reading and records of books lent outside. Registers covering 1475 to 1547 survive. Even in a famous manuscript collection, somebody had to know who had borrowed what: the missing-library-book problem is considerably older than a school backpack.

Melozzo da Forlì painted Sixtus IV with Platina and members of the pope’s family in the old library. The museum identifies papal nephews among the figures. This is a commissioned image of patronage and connections, not a neutral group photograph of everyone who worked there.

Santo Spirito’s foundling wheel allowed an infant to be placed inside and turned toward the hospital. A bell alerted the nuns, who arranged care with wet nurses. The institution dates the wheel’s presence cautiously, probably to the fifteenth century; the mechanism cannot supply the missing stories of every family.

The wheel’s opening limited the size of a child who could be passed through it. Older children could still be received through the hospital entrance. That practical detail matters: the device was one route into care, not a complete description of whom the hospital accepted.

The Acqua Felice works of the 1580s brought water to Rome’s hills, partly reusing an ancient aqueduct. The monumental Fountain of Moses advertised the achievement. Supplying elevated neighborhoods required engineering as well as a handsome fountain; this evidence does not mean every household had indoor running water.

A short inscription on the fountain reads “COEPIT PONT. AN. I ABSOLVIT III MDLXXXVII”: “He began in the first year of his pontificate; completed [it] in the third, 1587.” The Latin abbreviation and Roman numerals recorded construction in the pope’s regnal years. This is an attested inscription, transcribed by Rome’s heritage page.

The fountain’s Moses attracted criticism because he holds the tablets of the Law beside water coming from the rock, although the biblical episodes occur in a different order. Monumental art could get a very public editorial review. The criticism concerns the story being represented, not whether the waterworks functioned.

In 1555 Paul IV imposed the Roman ghetto and severe restrictions on Jewish residents, including forced residence and property sales. Families also faced identifying marks and limits on work. Papal patronage of beautiful churches and books coexisted with policies that constrained another community’s daily life.

ending.text: Italian forces captured Rome in 1870 and annexed the remaining papal territory. The Holy See continued as a religious and diplomatic institution. Vatican City was created by the 1929 Lateran settlement; it should not be substituted for the much larger historical Papal States or dated to the atlas’s 1878 endpoint.
